title: An app keeps access after its installer leaves
scenario: A former employee connected a reporting app to company files. The app still runs overnight.
question: Does the app act for a signed-in person or under its own permission grant? Who can review and revoke the grant?
proof: Identify the service principal, grant type and business owner. If access is no longer approved, verify the grant was removed and check available target activity and token lifetime.
limit: Tenant-wide admin consent and app-only access describe different things. Check both the permission type and who granted consent.

title: A former maintainer’s repository deploy key remains active
scenario: A contractor leaves, but the build server still reads a private repository using an SSH deploy key.
question: Which key is attached to the repository, which jobs use it, and who owns the private key now?
proof: Match the key fingerprint to a named job and owner. If the key is retired, document removal from the repository and a successful build using the intended replacement.
limit: Removing the person from the repository can leave the deploy key active. One healthy build does not prove the old key was removed.

title: An acquired employee has accounts in two tenants
scenario: During a merger, staff use synchronized accounts to access the parent’s applications. One person leaves while both directories are operating.
owner: Identity integration lead and target application owner
question: When HR ends employment, which directory event reaches the receiving tenant, and which local accounts still need follow-up?
proof: Trace a test leaver from the source event to the target account state and a representative application. Reconcile local accounts and grants outside synchronization.
limit: Entra documents different results for blocking sign-in and for deleting or removing a user from synchronization scope.

title: Rotation succeeds, but the next build prints the new secret
scenario: A developer enables verbose logging to debug a failed release. AppSec receives a report that an API key was visible in the build log.
owner: Developer security and the credential issuer
question: Who can access the log, what produced the output, and could the next run expose the replacement?
proof: Record issuer-side retirement of the exposed credential and handling of the affected log. Demonstrate a corrected test run with a synthetic marker and a healthy release.
limit: Cleaning up a log does not establish that previously accessible copies disappeared. Keep the credential value out of tickets and evidence.

title: A package has trusted publishing and an old automation token
scenario: The release team migrates an npm package to trusted publishing. A previous CI provider still holds an automation token.
question: Which identities and workflows can publish this package today, and which old credentials are still accepted?
proof: Review the package’s trusted publisher and token policy. Confirm the intended release path works, unnecessary legacy tokens were revoked and other packages using those tokens were accounted for.
limit: A successful trusted-publisher release confirms one working path. It leaves the status of other publishing credentials open.

title: A deal-room file stays accessible after named guests are removed
scenario: A deal closes and legal removes outside advisers from a shared folder. A financial model may still be available through a broadly shared link.
question: What access comes from named people, the parent folder and the file’s general link setting?
proof: Check effective sharing on the file and its parent. Confirm with an approved test identity or unsigned session that the former access path is closed while intended users retain access.
limit: Changing sharing settings cannot recall copies already downloaded. A public link alone also does not establish that anyone used it.

title: Can the company recover admin access during an identity outage?
scenario: The usual sign-in provider is unavailable during an incident. An emergency administrator needs access, and the SOC needs to know when it is used.
question: When was the recovery path last exercised without relying on the failed sign-in dependency, and who received the alert?
proof: In an authorized drill, verify the emergency account can perform its intended task, the expected alert reaches the SOC, and authorized custodians and recovery instructions are current.
limit: An account listed in a runbook is insufficient evidence that its authentication dependencies and alert routing work.

title: A cloud role session exists when access is withdrawn
scenario: An incident responder has removed a person’s ability to assume an AWS role. The team needs to account for sessions issued before that change.
question: Which sessions predate containment, and which legitimate workloads or responders share the same role?
proof: Record the role, cutoff and containment action or expiry. Review the impacted session window, any new grants and service health after the change.
limit: AWS documents that role-session revocation affects credentials for the role issued before the cutoff. A shared role can affect other users too.
